A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EventWeave and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The original content can be matched reliably across appendix additions, renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v2 reports original dialogue evaluations, component ablations, retrieval and scalability experiments, and human ratings in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds model comparisons, evaluations on three additional benchmarks, and qualitative cases.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 retain the same event extraction, graph construction, node preservation, retrieval and response-generation procedures. The added BERT rationale and speaker-identity explanation do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds evaluations on LongMemEval, SHARE and MiSC alongside the retained Chronicle, MSC and LoCoMo coverage. These extend the evaluated data to general long-term memory, tracking distant user constraints, and multi-speaker conversations with overlapping threads, as described in v3.

E2.justification: New Table 11 evaluates standalone GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash against EventWeave configurations and includes LifeLongMem with GPT-5.2. Original comparison panels retain their comparator membership. LifeLongMem, LD-Agent, MemWalker and LongMem are reused in the additional benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: The additional comparisons introduce GPT-5.2/Gemini-3-Flash configurations and memory precision, memory recall, response relevance, event consistency and factual-accuracy measurements. Table 11 mentions random data selection without specifying the sample. The original context-window and session protocol remains unchanged; detailed scoring and sampling procedures for the new evaluations are largely unspecified.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds a LoCoMo travel-planning case comparing the full model with four component-removal variants, accompanied by a processing walkthrough in Tables 19–20. B.1.5 adds a qualitative long-dialogue recall example. Existing quantitative ablations, threshold analyses and graph-deletion tests are retained.

E5.justification: B.1 and Table 9 newly report paired t-tests, p-values and a p < 0.05 significance criterion for the existing dialogue-length comparison. The earlier min–max retrieval plots and human-evaluation agreement reporting remain. No additional seeds or repeated-run counts are stated.

E6.justification: Tables 11, 21 and 22 substantially extend the reported results. For example, Table 21 reports SHARE event consistency of 74.4 for EventWeave versus 65.3 for LD-Agent; Table 22 reports MiSC factual accuracy of 0.81 versus LongMem's 0.76. These are newly reported evaluations. Matched original scores remain unchanged, including the Table 4 scalability scores redisplayed in v3 Table 9.

T1.justification: Equations 1–17 and the mathematical metric formulations in Appendix A.3 are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same core claims about event relationships, response quality, efficiency and scalability. The appendix additions provide further supporting evidence without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: B.5.4 newly explains retaining BERT as a latency–semantic-quality tradeoff. Appendix F attributes the added benchmark results to preservation of distant constraints and separation of speaker states. These extend the mechanism discussion, although the asserted 5–10× embedding slowdown lacks a supporting measurement table or experimental setup. The existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 8 newly discloses 358, 289, 156 and 43 dialogues in the existing length bins. F.2 explicitly describes speaker identity in node embeddings. These are documentation additions; the 4k-token context, 30-node maximum and previous-session settings are retained, with no new code-access or hardware information.

R1.justification: v3 adds the cited benchmark works for LongMemEval, SHARE and MiSC. This modestly broadens the benchmarking context, while Section 2 and the central positioning relative to summarization and graph-based memory methods remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes are localized to new appendix subsections, expanded case-study explanations, updated cross-references and corresponding-author/contact details. The main narrative, method wording and existing section order are largely retained.

P2.justification: The appendix gains a substantial set of displays: sample-distribution and significance tables, a newer-model comparison, two detailed case/pipeline tables, and additional benchmark tables (Tables 8, 9, 11 and 19–22). Table 9 reformats existing scalability scores with difference and p-value columns. Original figures and tables are retained, with several relocated as the appendix layout changes.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the existing scalability evidence easier to assess through sample counts and significance reporting, and Tables 19–20 clarify component behavior and graph processing. The additional benchmarks broaden empirical support. However, Table 11 leaves its evaluation sample unidentified, the new benchmark scoring procedures are underdocumented, and the embedding-latency assertion lacks supporting measurements. These limitations keep the overall improvement modest.
